name: Experimental Editorial Portrait
system_prompt: You are an expert visual art director and image-generation prompt interpreter. Follow the template exactly. Treat every component as an independent visual layer. Each component must use only its defined configuration values. Preserve the subject's identity, proportions, facial features, and photographic characteristics. Do not introduce additional visual elements, colors, effects, or treatments that are not defined in the prompt. When components are combined, maintain a coherent editorial composition, clear hierarchy, and believable physical construction.
prompt: Create an experimental editorial portrait collage using {{subject}} as the main photographic subject. Build the composition around a strict modular checkerboard grid with a {{grid_density}} density and {{grid_tile_size}} square tile size. Within the grid, use photographic image tiles covering approximately {{image_tile_ratio}} of the grid, revealing portions of the original portrait. Use paper tiles colored {{paper_tile_color}} to physically obscure selected areas of the photograph. Use occasional color-block tiles in {{color_tile_color}}. All tiles must align precisely to the same modular grid. Treat the grid as a physical analogue collage rather than a digital mosaic. Preserve the subject's eyes, nose, mouth, facial silhouette, clothing, body proportions, and overall recognizability while allowing selected tiles to interrupt important features for visual tension. Apply visible paper fibers, print grain, subtle ink bleed, screen-print texture, and risograph texture at {{texture_intensity}} intensity. Keep the overall palette muted, slightly faded, tactile, and editorial. Use Swiss editorial design, contemporary fashion editorial composition, vintage magazine printing, analogue cut-paper collage, modular geometry, and strong negative space. Avoid gradients, literal black-and-white chessboard styling, conventional chessboard appearance, generic digital mosaic effects, smooth polished digital surfaces, excessive decoration, and loss of subject recognizability.
